Research to inform the design of "Yildizim" — a closed-source, full-3D, browser-based, gamified galaxy visualization for a knowledge-base product (notes = planets orbiting vault-stars, grouped into project-galaxies). Cover three areas and synthesize findings into concrete, cited design recommendations:

1. EXISTING 3D/SPATIAL KNOWLEDGE VISUALIZATION TOOLS: How do tools like TheBrain, Kumu, Obsidian's 3D graph plugins/community plugins, VR/AR knowledge-mapping tools, and infinite-canvas tools (Kinopio, are.na, Muse, tldraw) handle: visual hierarchy at scale (hundreds/thousands of nodes), zoom transitions between detail and overview, labeling/readability in 3D space, and avoiding the generic "dark background with glowing nodes" AI-cliché look. What specifically makes some of these feel premium/breathtaking vs. generic?

2. GAMIFICATION AND NEGLECT/DECAY MECHANICS: How do products like Duolingo (streaks), the Forest app (a tree that dies if you leave the app — the closest existing precedent to a "your content decays if neglected" mechanic), GitHub's contribution graph, Strava, and habit-tracking apps design reward loops that motivate continued engagement without feeling manipulative or like corporate busywork? What achievement/sharing patterns actually get shared to social media organically vs. feel cringey? Any research or case studies on what makes a "negative" mechanic (decay, loss, a dying pet/plant) more motivating than a purely positive one (points only)?

3. GAMES WITH GALAXY-SCALE ZOOM AND PROCEDURAL SPACE: How do No Man's Sky, Spore, Elite Dangerous, Universe Sandbox, and Stellaris handle the visual and technical transition from viewing a single object (planet) up through solar system up through galaxy up through multi-galaxy views? How do they keep performance reasonable and the scene readable at each zoom level? What UI conventions do they use for information overlay (labels, stats) on top of a 3D space scene without cluttering it?

Also briefly note technical rendering considerations for implementing something like this in a web browser (e.g. Three.js/WebGL performance patterns for large dynamic node counts, level-of-detail techniques) — high-level only, this is for design research not implementation planning yet.

Synthesize into: a short summary of what's already been tried and what best practices emerge, and a set of concrete recommendations for Yildizim's specific design (galaxy/star/planet/moon hierarchy, decay mechanic, gamification/rewards, 3D navigation).

result.summary: Verified evidence is strongest for gamification/decay mechanics, moderate for game-derived 3D navigation conventions, and thin for existing knowledge-visualization tools. Two independent peer-reviewed studies converge on a clear pattern: loss-aversion framing tied to something a user has actively earned (not handed to them) drives measurably stronger completion/engagement behavior than pure positive-points systems, but fixed/positive reward scores higher on self-reported enjoyment — so a "planet dies from neglect" mechanic should threaten earned state, not a starter state, and needs positive counterweight. Forest's tree-death is the closest real precedent for decay-not-block, and dark-pattern ethics literature places loss+urgency+scarcity messaging on the edge of manipulative "social engineering," arguing for transparent, player-visible decay timers rather than surprise punishment. For 3D navigation, only small-scale interaction patterns survived verification — proximity-fading labels, hover-triggered side-panel stats, and nested zoom with dual schematic/to-scale views (Elite Dangerous) — while every claim about solving visual hierarchy/clutter at true galaxy scale (hundreds/thousands of nodes, in any tool examined) was refuted, leaving Yildizim's central visual-design problem without a verified precedent. No Man's Sky's staged voxel-to-simulation generation pipeline is a real precedent for scale-dependent level of detail, but its "seamless, loading-free" transition claim did not survive verification.
result.caveats: Area 1 (existing spatial knowledge-viz tools) came back thin: TheBrain, Kumu, VR/AR knowledge-mapping tools, are.na, Muse, and tldraw produced zero surviving claims. Several plausible-sounding mechanisms were specifically tested and refuted, not just unfound — degree-based node sizing (Obsidian plugin), bounded-page infinite canvas theory, Muse's four spatial-memory constraints, and Kinopio's "memory palace" cognitive rationale. Do not assume any of these are actually how those tools work; treat them as open. The galaxy-scale (thousands-of-node) visual-hierarchy question — Yildizim's core design problem — is unverified everywhere it was tested: Elite Dangerous's own Galaxy Map claims about color-coding and hover-only decluttering at scale were both refuted (0-3). The confirmed Elite Dangerous claims only cover single-system-level interaction (one star's info panel, one system's zoom/orrery toggle), not galaxy-map clutter management — the navigation/label recommendations below are validated at small scale and extrapolated to galaxy scale, not proven there. The core gamification numbers (18.4pp, 10.61pp) come from one RCT (n=602, step-tracking app); the 18.4pp figure specifically had a 2-1 split vote, weaker than the 3-0 10.61pp and earned-vs-endowed conclusion — lead with the latter two if citing this study. The cybersecurity-training corroboration is a different domain with a small sample (n=27); it corroborates direction (loss framing wins on outcome, fixed reward wins on engagement) not magnitude. No Man's Sky's "seamless, no loading break" claim was refuted (1-2 vote) — only the staged-pipeline architecture itself is supported. Duolingo streaks, GitHub's contribution graph, and Strava — the sharing/virality half of the gamification question — produced zero surviving claims and are entirely unanswered by this research pass. Several sources are Fandom wikis or a single creator's personal blog (Kinopio); corroborated by secondary search but not official documentation, and version-specific software details (plugin behavior, game UI) can drift with updates in a way the behavioral-econ findings (2020-2025) do not.

findings.claim: 3D graph tools solve label clutter with proximity-based disclosure — labels fade in only when the camera nears a node and fade out as it retreats — rather than showing all labels at once or relying on node size to convey hierarchy.
findings.evidence: "When you are closer to the node, the label will appear. When you move away from the node, the node will fade away." A related claim that the same plugin sizes nodes by connection-degree to establish hierarchy was explicitly refuted (0-3) — so label-proximity-fade is confirmed, automatic size-based hierarchy is not. Design implication for Yildizim: use camera-distance-driven label opacity for star/planet/moon names at all zoom tiers instead of persistent text, but don't assume node-size-by-importance alone will solve galaxy-scale legibility — that mechanism has no verified support.

findings.claim: Professional/power-user spatial tools deliberately expose controls rather than hiding them behind minimal, chic UI — Kinopio's creator frames this as a race-car/synthesizer principle: at high engagement intensity, accessible buttons beat a clean hidden menu.
findings.evidence: "If you were going 200mph would you rather find your controls inside a clean/minimal/aesthetic menu, or just hit some upfront buttons and dials?" — the tool's own creator rejecting minimalism-as-default for serious/frequent users. Design implication: Yildizim is a knowledge tool used repeatedly by engaged users, not a one-off marketing site — resist over-minimizing the UI chrome (stats, controls) purely for a cinematic look; this is also a lever against the generic 'dark background, nothing but glowing nodes' AI-cliché, which often results from stripping away all functional UI in favor of pure atmosphere.

findings.claim: In a 602-person RCT on a fitness app, loss aversion tied to an already-earned gamification tier is a stronger behavioral lever than either a no-gamification control or simply offering more points to gain: being at risk of losing an earned status, and having a real chance to advance a level, both beat a plain control, and the mechanism only works when the threatened status was earned through effort, not when it was handed to the user for free.
findings.evidence: Three findings from the same trial: (a) "Participants who could potentially move from the low to the medium level were 10.61% (95% CI: 9.98-11.24) more likely to meet their step goal" than a no-gamification control [3-0]; (b) participants at risk of losing their highest earned level were "18.40% (95% CI: 18.26-19.90) more likely to meet their step goal" than those with nothing left to lose [2-1, weaker vote — treat as supporting, not headline]; (c) the paper's own conclusion: "participants in this trial generally exhibit loss aversion so long as the loss relates to something that was earned rather than endowed" [3-0]. Design implication: Yildizim's decay mechanic should threaten a status the user actively built (a planet they grew, a level they climbed), never a default/starter state handed out for free — endowed loss doesn't move behavior in this study. Both 'climb to unlock' and 'at risk of losing what's unlocked' are real motivators, with loss-of-earned-status the stronger single lever, though that specific number is the less certain of the two.

findings.claim: A second, independent study (cybersecurity training, n=27) corroborates the direction of the fitness-app finding but adds an important trade-off: loss-aversion framing produced better learning/behavioral outcomes than fixed positive-only rewards, but fixed reward scored higher on self-reported user engagement/enjoyment — the paper's own conclusion is that neither mechanic is universally better, suitability depends on context.
findings.evidence: "Findings indicate that while LA was more effective in improving cyber security knowledge, FR received higher scores for user engagement... both LA and FR offer distinct advantages, with suitability depending on the specific training context." Design implication: don't build Yildizim's reward system on decay/loss alone — it likely drives more usage but risks feeling less enjoyable/more punishing than a purely positive system. Pair the decay mechanic with genuinely positive moments (visual 'bloom'/growth rewards, streak milestones) so the app isn't purely aversive. Note this is a small-sample study in a different domain (security training, not personal knowledge tools) — it corroborates direction, not exact magnitude, of the fitness-app RCT above.

findings.claim: Dark-pattern / UX-ethics literature explicitly defines exploiting fear of loss, urgency, and scarcity to control user behavior as 'social engineering,' a manipulative design category — and separately argues gamification designers have an ethical responsibility to build transparency with users rather than manipulate them, since gamification dark patterns are described as directly borrowed from e-commerce manipulation tactics.
findings.evidence: PMC review: "Social Engineering... a strategy that uses socio-psychological mechanisms to influence and control usage behavior. These mechanisms can include the need for belonging, fear of loss, or the reaction to urgency and scarcity." Goethe/CRC Press chapter: "...designers are using creative yet deceiving UX to manipulate the user-behavior and achieve their objectives" and the chapter's thesis that "gamification designers must be responsible for their actions, while focusing on establishing transparency with the users rather than manipulating them." Design implication: a decay mechanic sits directly on top of the fear-of-loss + urgency taxonomy this literature calls manipulative. Yildizim should make decay rules fully visible and predictable up front (e.g., a clearly shown 'this planet fades after N days of no visits' state, not a hidden countdown surfaced only via a guilt-inducing push notification), and avoid artificial scarcity/urgency copy ('come back now or lose everything!') that would read as social engineering rather than a fair game mechanic.

findings.claim: Forest is the closest existing real-world precedent for a 'content decays if neglected' mechanic: its core loop is a tree that visibly withers and dies if the user leaves the app before a timer completes, using psychological loss/guilt rather than a hard technical block on access.
findings.evidence: "the tree withers if the user opens another application before the timer ends" — corroborated by independent reviews describing this as a deliberate loss-aversion mechanism, explicitly contrasted with hard app-blockers that lock access outright. Design implication: model Yildizim's decay visually the same way — a planet dims/shrinks/loses atmosphere over time rather than the app blocking or deleting anything. Decay should be a felt, reversible visual state (evokes guilt/motivation to return) not a punitive access restriction or data loss.

findings.claim: No Man's Sky's continuous zoom from space down to a planet's surface is technically built on a staged procedural-generation pipeline — voxel-based generation, then polygonization into a mesh, then texturing, then population/simulation — a concrete pattern for scale-dependent level of detail. Its transition being 'seamless with no loading break' was not confirmed by this research.
findings.evidence: "a step-by-step breakdown of their generation pipeline, from voxel-based world generation, through polygonization and texturing, to eventual population and simulation." A separate, stronger claim that this pipeline delivers a seamless, loading-screen-free transition between space and planet views was tested and refuted (1-2 vote) — the underlying architecture is real and precedented, but this research did not substantiate that the player-facing result is imperceptibly smooth. Design implication for Yildizim's rendering approach (high-level, not implementation): swap representation fidelity by zoom tier — coarse/point-sprite representation at galaxy view, detailed mesh/material only near the camera — is a standard, precedented pattern (general LOD/imposter technique, reinforced by this NMS case study), but budget for and test transition seams explicitly rather than assuming staged generation alone guarantees a seamless feel.

findings.claim: Elite Dangerous's UI conventions for a single star system are: (1) detailed per-object stats live in a dedicated hover-triggered Info side-panel rather than as in-scene floating text, gated behind data the player has 'purchased'/discovered; (2) the System Map offers two toggleable display modes — a simplified schematic 'Map' and a to-scale 3D 'Orrery' with real orbits/distances; (3) the map supports nested zoom from full system view down into individual landable planet/moon surfaces, with an explicit zoom-out action to return to the system view.
findings.evidence: "The Info tab displays information about the system that the mouse is currently hovering over... when you have access to this data (i.e. purchased it)." "There are two display modes: the default 'Map'... and 'Orrery', which displays a 3D model of the system with orbits and distances." "...the ability to further zoom in to landable planets and moons, and examine their surfaces in detail... The Planetary Map can be exited by zooming back out to the full System Map." Note: broader claims that Elite Dangerous solves galaxy-scale (thousands-of-system) clutter via hover-only overlays or color-coding were refuted (0-3 each) — these confirmed conventions are single-system-scale, not proven at galaxy scale. Design implication: give Yildizim a 'schematic' galaxy/project view for fast overview navigation and a separate 'to-scale, orbit-accurate' vault-star view for immersion, toggle-able rather than forced; use a hover-driven side-panel (not in-scene text) for star/planet stats; support drill-down zoom (galaxy -> vault-star -> note-planet -> moon) with an explicit, discoverable zoom-out control at every level, not just pinch/scroll-to-exit.

openQuestions: How do TheBrain, Kumu, and VR/AR knowledge-mapping tools actually manage visual hierarchy and label clutter at hundreds-to-thousands-of-node scale? No claims about these tools survived verification — this remains completely open.

What specific art-direction techniques (lighting, material choice, color grading, composition, motion) distinguish a 'premium/breathtaking' 3D space UI from the generic AI dark-background-with-glowing-nodes cliché? No surviving claim addressed this question directly despite it being explicitly asked.

What achievement/sharing patterns actually get shared to social media organically versus feel cringey — covering Duolingo streaks, GitHub's contribution graph, and Strava kudos/segments specifically? Zero claims from this research cluster survived verification; this half of the gamification question is unanswered.

Does any tool have a verified mechanism for gracefully degrading visual complexity as node count scales into the thousands (true galaxy-scale clutter management), as opposed to the single-system/single-node interaction patterns that did survive verification? This is the central open gap for Yildizim's core visual-design problem.

refuted.claim: Node visual size is dynamically scaled by degree of connection (more links = bigger node), used as the plugin's mechanism for establishing visual hierarchy among hundreds/thousands of nodes without manual styling.

No Man's Sky's procedural pipeline lets players transition seamlessly between a space view and interactive, populated planetary terrain with no apparent loading break, directly relevant to Yildizim's galaxy-to-star-to-planet zoom design.

Elite Dangerous's Galaxy Map avoids cluttering the 3D space view with persistent data overlays by surfacing system information only on hover, via a contextual menu and a separate side panel (Info tab), rather than always-on labels.

At galaxy scale (thousands of star systems), Elite Dangerous manages visual hierarchy/readability primarily through color-coding systems and trade routes by category (allegiance, population, economy, commodity type) rather than through labels or increased geometric detail.

Information overlay in the 3D scene is kept uncluttered by making labels/stats appear only on demand via cursor hover, rather than persistently rendering data for every object; undiscovered objects are shown with a generic placeholder state instead of empty or missing UI.
Infinite canvas tools benefit from a bounded 'page' concept because pure infinite space removes the user's sense of scale and orientation
Giving users more open canvas space reduces their tendency to create nested sub-boards, which trades easier content creation for worse long-term readability/navigability at scale

Muse's canvas design uses four constraints to preserve spatial memory: boards anchor in the upper-left, the board is always sized to its content, scrolling into empty space is prevented, and zooming is disallowed to maintain a single scale level.
Infinite canvases without enforced borders/permanence fail to build spatial memory because item positions aren't guaranteed stable between visits, unlike a physical desk.
The creator justifies Kinopio's spatial/place-based canvas interface by appealing to human cognition being inherently spatial (memory palace-style reasoning), rather than list- or hierarchy-based UI.
